analysis.one_liner: Requires makers of cribs, strollers, and small appliances to keep recall-notification lists so owners learn of recalls.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with no cosponsors, was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee and died there without ever getting a vote when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The Consumer Product Safety Commission recalls about 300 hazardous products a year, but it can only warn the public through news reports and stores because manufacturers rarely know who bought their products—contact information is known for fewer than 7 percent of products sold. This bill would have directed the Commission to require manufacturers of children's products (cribs, strollers, high chairs, playpens) and small household appliances (toasters, blenders, coffee makers) to include a simple registration card or online signup with each product, and to keep a database used only to tell owners when a product is recalled. The bill was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee on August 1, 2002, and no further action was ever taken before the 107th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Families with young children and owners of small appliances benefit. When a crib or a blender is recalled, the manufacturer could contact registered owners directly—CPSC research found direct contact is one of the most effective ways to get consumers to act on a recall—instead of relying on the chance that people see a news story.

how_it_helps.text: The bill requires manufacturers of juvenile products and small household appliances to create a customer database used solely to notify consumers of recalls, through a simplified owner card, internet registration, or other methods like electronic tags [S3].

The bill's findings note that contact information exists for generally less than 7 percent of consumer products sold, so most recall warnings reach people only through media and retailers; direct consumer contact was found to be one of the most effective ways to motivate response to a recall [S3].

The bill bans marketing questions and personal-information requests on the owner cards—CPSC found most consumers don't return registration cards because they fear junk mail—so the cards would collect only the minimum contact information needed for recalls [S3].
It sets deadlines: a proposed rule within 90 days of enactment and a final rule within 270 days, with authority to exclude low-cost items for good cause [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Manufacturers of children's products and small appliances bear the cost of printing and processing registration cards or building registration systems and databases, costs that would partly pass into product prices.

drawbacks.text: The mandate adds a real cost to every covered product—printing cards, processing registrations, and maintaining databases—which falls hardest on makers of low-margin small appliances, even with the bill's option to exclude cheap items [S3].
Creating manufacturer-held databases of consumer buyers raises privacy concerns; the bill limits database use to recall notification only, but the data still has to be stored somewhere [S3].

Registration cards historically get a low response rate; the bill improves on this with simplified, marketing-free cards and electronic options, but even a workable system would never reach all owners, so recall gaps would remain [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The safety benefit is real but targeted: better recall notification for cribs, strollers, and small appliances, where defects can injure children. The cost is a modest compliance burden on manufacturers, largely passed into small price increases. A reasonable trade-off on its face, though the bill leaves the hard problem—getting consumers to register in the first place—to incentives and electronic options rather than guarantees.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee the day it was introduced, got no cosponsors, no hearing, and no vote, and expired when the 107th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Mary Landrieu introduced the bill on August 1, 2002, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation the same day [S5].
No cosponsors ever signed on to the bill [S4].
The full action history shows only introduction, sponsor introductory remarks, and the committee referral—no hearings, no markup, no floor action [S5].
The Congress ended on January 3, 2003, so the bill died in committee [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Manufacturers of juvenile products and small appliances are better off because the bill died—they avoided the cost of building recall-notification registration systems. Families with young children are left with a recall system that still reaches few product owners directly.

for.name: Sen. Mary Landrieu
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and made introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral—no hearing, no markup, no report—so it never reached the floor.

against.name: Sen. Ernest Hollings
against.role: Chair, Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never scheduled the bill for committee consideration before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor and no cosponsors of either party, and no vote was ever taken, so no party split can be measured.

industries.industry: Juvenile product manufacturers (cribs, strollers, high chairs, playpens)
industries.note: The bill would have required them to include registration cards or electronic registration with every product and maintain a recall-notification database. The compliance cost is real, but better recall notices directly protect their own customers and reduce child injuries—and the industry's interest here runs with the public's.

industries.industry: Small household appliance makers (toasters, blenders, coffee makers)
industries.note: They would have faced the same registration and database mandate on low-margin products. Safer recalls reduce injury and liability, but the per-unit cost of the system is the price.

Retailers currently serve as the main recall-alert channel; direct manufacturer notification would have shifted part of that burden to manufacturers while potentially improving recall compliance through stores as well.
